analysis.one_liner: Creates government-funded jobs for the unemployed, paid for by a tax on stock and bond trades.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with 43 House sponsors in February 2015, it sat in two committees until the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Full Employment Trust Fund financed by a new tax on securities trades — 0.2% on stock trades and 0.06% on bonds and derivatives. Most of the money would flow as grants to states, cities, schools, and nonprofits to hire unemployed people for community work — child care, home repair, parks, emergency food, environmental cleanup — at pay comparable to similar local jobs. The rest would fund existing workforce training programs. If unemployment rose despite the fund, the Federal Reserve would be directed to lend it additional money.
analysis.who_benefits: Unemployed and underemployed workers: people receiving unemployment insurance, the long-term unemployed, targeted groups, and part-timers seeking full-time work. Communities with high unemployment, poverty, vacancy, and poor health would get priority for jobs building and staffing public services. Labor unions are protected from displacement by strict no-substitution rules.

how_it_helps.text: Creates jobs for people who qualify by receiving unemployment insurance, being unemployed 30–60 days and actively seeking work, or being involuntarily part-time for 13 weeks [S3].

Guarantees at least 12 months of employment, 35–40 hours if full-time is wanted, and pay equal to what public-sector or comparable private-sector workers earn locally, with prevailing wages for construction [S3].

Requires grant recipients to spend at least 80% of project funds on wages, benefits, and support services like child care, and at least 35% of hires must be from the most disadvantaged eligibility groups [S3].
Bars funded jobs from replacing laid-off employees or undercutting union contracts, and gives workers binding arbitration and a Labor Department whistleblower hotline to enforce the rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Trading firms, exchanges, and brokers, who would remit a 0.2% tax on stock transfers and 0.06% on bond and derivative transactions; ordinary investors could bear part of it indirectly through higher trading costs. Taxpayers generally would not pay, except that the fund could borrow from the Federal Reserve during downturns.

drawbacks.text: A permanent public-jobs program of this scale is a large, open-ended federal commitment; the bill caps annual grant spending at 90% of tax revenue but lets the Federal Reserve lend the fund whatever is needed to hold unemployment in a 1-point range, an unusually direct role for the central bank [S3].

The trading tax would be collected on every covered transaction, which independent research commonly shows raises trading costs; retirement and mutual fund investors are exempted from the tax itself but could still see indirect cost increases [S3].

The bill includes an inflation brake: if unemployment falls below 4% while inflation exceeds 3%, hiring can be suspended and wages frozen, meaning the guarantee turns off exactly when the economy is strong [S3].

Eligibility hurdles — certification by a state employment service and required job search — would keep some jobless people out of the program, and workers must accept a suitable outside job or face disqualification [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: a guaranteed job at decent pay for anyone unemployed, funded by a tax that falls overwhelmingly on high-volume financial trading. The design includes unusually strong protections against displacing existing or union jobs. But the program's total cost depends entirely on how much trading occurs, the Federal Reserve lending provision is a novel and untested financing mechanism, and the inflation trigger could suspend hiring in downturns' aftermath. The trading tax's incidence — how much lands on big institutions versus ordinary retirement savers — was not resolved in the text.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and to a subcommittee in April 2015, it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers Jr. introduced the bill on February 13, 2015, joined by 42 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On April 29, 2015, it was referred to the Higher Education and Workforce Training subcommittee, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms that would have paid the new trading tax avoided it, and no jobs program was created; the unemployed gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that avoided the trading tax

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 43 supporters was a Democrat; the Republican-led committees it was sent to took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill's entire funding comes from a 0.2% tax on stock transfers and 0.06% tax on bond and derivative transactions, collected by exchanges and brokers. Its industry cost is the public's benefit: every dollar of the jobs fund comes from this tax.

industries.industry: Nonprofit community organizations and public schools
industries.note: They are the eligible grant recipients and would hire the workers, expanding child care, food programs, park maintenance, and school staffing in high-unemployment communities.
States, tribes, and local governments qualify for grants to fund community jobs and workforce training, adding staff for public services without local tax increases.

The bill bars funded jobs from displacing laid-off workers or violating collective bargaining agreements, and requires union consent where contracts cover similar work — protections designed to keep the program from undercutting organized labor.
